transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. I'm Dr. [Your Name]. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Hi, Doctor. Yeah, thank you. Well, I... I guess I came in because things have just been really, really heavy lately, and I just can't seem to shake this feeling I have. It's mostly about my family, you know? We took on this mortgage, and I just keep thinking about it, turning it over and over in my head every single day, and I just feel like I've completely let them down by doing it. It's this massive financial weight, and I just feel so incredibly guilty for putting us in this position when I don't know if I can handle it. 

And it just bleeds into absolutely everything else I do. Like, I'll be at work—I wait tables—and I'll make just a tiny, stupid mistake. You know, forgetting to ring in a side of dressing, or dropping a napkin, or getting a table number slightly wrong. Just really small things. But instead of just brushing it off like anyone else would, it just... it completely wrecks me. It just proves to me that I'm completely useless. I just stand there feeling like I'm a total failure and that I absolutely deserve whatever bad things happen to me, because if I can't even get the small things right at a restaurant, how am I supposed to handle a house and provide for my family? I just feel so worthless all the time, and it's just exhausting to carry that around every minute of the day, so I finally decided I needed to come talk to someone about it.
Have you noticed yourself losing interest in things you usually enjoy, like hobbies, time with family, or other activities?

No, I wouldn't really say I've lost interest, no. I mean, I still like doing the things I've always liked doing. Like, for example, I've always been really into fixing up old bicycles. It actually started a few years ago when we were trying to save a little money, and I figured I could just buy a used bike for my kid and fix it up instead of buying a brand new one. And I still really like doing that. I was actually out in the garage just this past Sunday—well, actually, wait, it was Saturday afternoon, right after my lunch shift ended at the restaurant—working on this old Schwinn I found at a garage sale a couple weeks back. I still get a real kick out of getting the rust off the spokes and getting the gears shifting smoothly again, you know? 

And I still really look forward to hanging out with my family, too. Like, every Friday night we have this tradition where we do a movie night. We make popcorn on the stove, not the microwave kind, because my wife swears the microwave kind is terrible for you, which, you know, she's probably right about that. So I still enjoy all of those things. It's not that I don't care about my hobbies or my family, or that I don't want to participate. I definitely still want to. 

It's just that... while I'm doing them, you know, sitting there watching the movie on the couch or scrubbing a greasy bike chain with a toothbrush, my brain is just constantly running a million miles an hour about the mortgage and the money and what a massive screw-up I am for putting us in this situation. So the interest in the actual activity is definitely still there, 100 percent. I still want to do those things. I just feel absolutely terrible and guilty while I'm doing them, if that makes any sense? So, yeah, I haven't lost interest, I just... I can't enjoy the interest the way I'm supposed to, I guess. I don't know if that really answers what you were asking.
Can you tell me if you've been feeling down or depressed most of the day, nearly every day, even when you're doing things you normally enjoy?

Yeah, I mean... yeah, that's exactly it. It's almost every single day, most of the day, just this... this really heavy, empty feeling right here in the middle of my chest. It's hard to describe, but it's like a physical weight, you know? Like I swallowed a rock or something. And it's just there, all the time. 

Like, I'll be at the restaurant—we get really busy on Tuesday nights because they do this two-for-one burger special, which honestly is a nightmare for the kitchen, but it brings in a ton of people—and I'll be out there on the floor, carrying these massive trays of plates, and I'm smiling at the customers, asking them how their day is going, filling up their water glasses, doing all the things a good waiter is supposed to do. But I'm just totally going through the motions. I'm smiling because I have to, because if I don't, I won't get good tips, and if I don't get good tips, how am I going to pay that mortgage I was telling you about? 

But inside, behind the smile, I just don't feel anything good. It's just that heavy emptiness. Even when a customer tells a joke or something funny happens, I might laugh, but it doesn't reach anywhere inside me. It's just this constant, low-level ache that never really lifts, from the minute I wake up and make my coffee—I usually have a cup of dark roast before I even talk to anyone—until I finally go to sleep. It's just always there, dragging me down, no matter what I'm doing or who I'm with. So yeah, "down" or "depressed" is probably the right word for it, because it's just this relentless, heavy emptiness that I can't seem to escape from.
Have you been feeling fatigued or lacking energy almost every day, even when you haven’t been doing anything physically or mentally taxing?

No, I wouldn't say I'm lacking energy, really. I mean, my job keeps me on my feet all day. Waitressing—well, waiting tables, I guess I should say—is a really physical job, more than people realize. You're constantly moving, carrying those heavy trays like I mentioned before, rushing from the kitchen to the floor, weaving between tables. And I still have the energy to do all that. I'm not dragging my feet or feeling like I need a nap in the middle of a shift, even on a double when I work lunch and dinner back-to-back. 

And even on my days off, I'm not just lying around in bed or anything. Like I said, I was out in the garage working on that bicycle on Saturday, scrubbing the rust off, which takes a fair amount of elbow grease, you know? And I still help out around the house, doing the yard work, mowing the lawn, trimming the hedges—we have these overgrown bushes by the front porch that I'm always having to hack back because otherwise they block the walkway. 

So physically, my energy levels feel pretty normal. It's not like I'm exhausted or fatigued in my body. It's more just... it's all in my head, you know? It's that heavy feeling in my chest and the constant worrying about the mortgage and feeling like a failure. That's what's exhausting, the mental part of it. But as far as physical energy goes, no, I haven't noticed any drop in that. I can still get up and do everything I need to do, it's just that I feel terrible while I'm doing it. So I wouldn't say I'm fatigued in the way you're asking about, no.
Have you noticed any changes in your appetite or weight lately, like eating more or less than usual?

Well, my eating has definitely been... it's been all over the place, honestly. It's really erratic. Like, there are some weeks where I just don't have any appetite at all. At the restaurant, they give us a staff meal before the dinner rush starts, usually around 4:30 or 5:00, and normally I'd eat a full plate of whatever the kitchen threw together—like pasta or a burger or whatever. But lately, on those bad weeks, I'll just stare at it. I'll maybe pick at a few fries or take one bite of chicken, and that's it. My stomach just feels completely tied in knots, probably from all the worrying about the house and the money, and the thought of swallowing food just seems impossible. I'll just drink water or maybe some soda to keep my blood sugar up so I don't pass out on the floor, but I barely touch the actual food.

But then, it swings completely the other way. There are other nights where I get home after a closing shift—and closing shifts are brutal, you're there until 1:00 or 2:00 in the morning sometimes, rolling silverware and wiping down the stations—and I'll walk in the door and just eat whatever I can find in the kitchen. I'm not even really hungry, it's more like I'm just trying to fill up that empty, heavy feeling in my chest that I was telling you about earlier. I'll eat a bowl of cereal, then half a sleeve of crackers, maybe some leftover pizza if my wife left any in the fridge... just anything to try and feel settled, you know? To try and make the anxiety and the emptiness quiet down for a few minutes so I can actually fall asleep. So yeah, my appetite is just completely unpredictable right now. I haven't really been tracking my weight on a scale or anything, but my pants definitely feel a little looser some weeks and then tighter on others, depending on which way my eating is swinging. It's just a constant back-and-forth.
Have you noticed yourself moving or speaking more slowly than usual, or on the flip side, feeling restless or unable to sit still, like you need to keep moving?

Well, it's funny you ask that, because I wouldn't have really noticed it myself if people at work hadn't started pointing it out to me. But yeah, it's been happening, and it's kind of embarrassing, honestly. Like, my manager, Dave—he's been managing the place for like fifteen years, so he notices everything—he pulled me aside the other day during the lunch rush. And the lunch rush is usually pretty chaotic, you know, people trying to get in and out on their lunch breaks, so you have to move fast. But Dave was like, "Hey man, are you okay? You're pacing around like a caged tiger." 

And I didn't even realize I was doing it, but I was. I was just walking back and forth, checking the same tables over and over, making sure the salt and pepper shakers were perfectly aligned, looking at the same receipts three or four times to make sure I hadn't messed up a charge, even though I knew I hadn't. It's like I just couldn't stand still. My body just felt this... this weird need to keep moving, like there was this nervous energy trapped inside me, even though I'm so exhausted mentally. I'd be tapping my foot at the server station, rearranging the sugar packets, just doing anything to keep my hands and feet busy. 

But then, and this is the really weird part, it swings completely the other way sometimes. Like, later that same week, I was working a dinner shift, and we had a big party of twelve come in—a birthday party, I think, they brought their own cake, which we're supposed to charge a plating fee for, but I always feel bad doing that. Anyway, I was supposed to be grabbing menus and bringing them over, and I just... I felt like I was moving through molasses. It was like my legs weighed a hundred pounds each. I was walking to the POS system to ring in their drink orders, and it just felt like it was taking me forever to get there. One of the other servers, Jessica, actually bumped into me because I was walking so slow, and she made a joke about me needing another cup of coffee. But it wasn't that I was tired, not physically anyway. It was just this heaviness, like my brain was telling my body to move, but the signal was getting lost somewhere along the way. Reaching for the menus, punching the buttons on the screen... it all just felt so slow and deliberate, like I had to think about every single movement before I made it. So yeah, I guess I've been doing a bit of both, the pacing around and the moving really slow, depending on the day or even the hour.
Have you ever felt like life isn’t worth living, or had thoughts about not wanting to live anymore?

Well... I mean, that’s a heavy question, but I want to be completely honest with you. I don't have a plan to hurt myself or anything like that. I really need you to know that right off the bat, because I would never actually do anything—I couldn't do that to my wife, leaving her to deal with the mortgage and all the mess on her own. So no, no plans, I'm not going to do anything. 

But... well, it’s like I was saying about those restaurant shifts. Sometimes they have me on the opening shift, which means I have to be there at 6:00 AM to start brewing the coffee, rolling the patio umbrellas out, and making sure the server stations are stocked before we unlock the doors. And when I’m lying awake before an early shift like that... usually it's around 3:30 or 4:00 in the morning, and the house is completely quiet, and I'm just staring up at the ceiling fan in the dark, watching the red numbers on the alarm clock change... my mind just goes to these really dark places. 

I'll just be lying there, listening to my wife breathe next to me, and I sometimes think it would just be so much easier if I just didn’t wake up. Like, if I could just slip away in my sleep and not have to face the day. Because waking up means I have to get out of bed, put on my uniform, tie my apron, and go out there and just... keep failing at everything. That's exactly what it feels like, you know? Like I'm just constantly failing—at my job, at providing for us, at keeping the house together, at just being a normal functioning person. The thought of having to do it all over again, pasting on a fake smile for customers and asking if they want sparkling or still water while I feel so incredibly heavy inside... it's just so exhausting. 

So yeah, I don't want to kill myself, I don't have a plan, but in those quiet hours before the sun comes up, the idea of just not waking up and not having to try so hard anymore... it just seems like it would be a relief. It really does.
Have you noticed a significant decrease in interest or pleasure in almost all activities, even those you used to enjoy?

Well, no, I wouldn't say that. Actually, that's one of the few things that hasn't gone sideways on me lately. I mean, even with everything else going on—the weird appetite, the pacing around at work, lying awake at four in the morning feeling like a total failure—I still actually really enjoy my downtime. 

Like, my main thing outside of the restaurant is my record collection. I've been collecting vinyl since I was taking classes at the community college, back before it got super trendy and expensive again, you know? And I still get a huge kick out of it. Just this past Sunday, which is usually my one guaranteed day off unless someone calls out sick and Dave begs me to cover, I spent like three hours down at this little vintage shop on 4th Street. They have these dollar bins in the very back, and you have to literally get on your hands and knees to dig through them because they're shoved under the main display tables. It smells like dust and old paper, but I absolutely love it. I found this old jazz album I’ve been looking for, and I was genuinely thrilled. 

I brought it home, cleaned it up with my special velvet brush—you have to be really careful with the grooves on the older pressings, especially if they've been sitting in a basement somewhere—and I just sat in the living room listening to the whole thing front to back. My wife was reading on the couch, and it was just... it was really nice. I still felt that exact same excitement I always do when the needle drops and you hear that little crackle. 

So, yeah, even though I've been feeling so heavy and exhausted, and the worrying is just eating away at me, I haven't lost my interest in the things I actually like doing. If anything, I think I cling to them a bit more right now because it's the only time my brain kind of quiets down. I still like my records, I still enjoy watching baseball if I catch a game on the TV at the bar, I still like making a nice Sunday breakfast for me and my wife when I have the morning off... so no, I haven't lost interest in that stuff. It's really just the rest of my life that feels so overwhelming.
Would you say that your depressed mood is present most of the day, nearly every day?

Well, yeah... I guess if I really take a step back and look at it, it is pretty much every day. Most of the day, too. It’s... it’s hard to describe exactly, but most days there’s just this heavy, empty feeling right in the middle of my chest. It’s almost like a physical weight, you know? Like a void that just sits there while I'm trying to go about my life. 

And it just doesn't really go away. Like, I’ll be at work, right? And I'm carrying these massive trays of food—we use these thick, rustic ceramic plates at the restaurant that weigh an absolute ton, especially when you’re balancing three or four entrees on one arm—and I’m just completely going through the motions. I'm walking out of the kitchen, setting down the plates, and I'm putting on this big, friendly smile for the customers. I'm saying, 'Here you go, folks, can I get you some extra napkins or another round of drinks?' But I’m only smiling because I’m supposed to. Because Dave is always watching the floor, and because if you don't smile, your tips go down the drain, and my wife and I really need the money to keep up with the bills. 

But behind that smile, I don't feel anything good at all. There's no spark, no connection with the people I'm talking to. It’s just that constant, empty heaviness. I'm just acting out the part of a waiter. Whether it’s 11:00 AM and I’m just clocking in and setting up the patio, or it’s 9:00 PM and I’m finally rolling silverware and counting my cash to go home, that feeling is just... there. It doesn't matter what I'm doing, I'm just lugging that emptiness around with me. So yeah, to answer your question, it's pretty much a constant thing all day, almost every single day.
Have you noticed any trouble concentrating or thinking clearly lately, like your mind feels slowed down or you're having a hard time focusing on tasks?

Yeah, actually... it's funny you bring that up because it's been driving me absolutely crazy at work, and it's making me feel even worse about everything. My brain just feels like it's wading through thick mud lately. 

Like, we use this really outdated POS system at the restaurant—Point of Sale, the computers where we punch in all the food and drink orders—and it's one of those older touchscreens where the layout is just a total mess of tiny colored buttons. I've been working there for years, right? I know this system like the back of my hand. I know exactly where the button for the side of ranch is, or how to ring in a weird allergy modification without even looking. But lately... I’m just having so much trouble keeping the numbers straight. 

I'll be standing there at the terminal, and I'll punch in a completely standard order for a four-top, and then I just... I freeze. I will literally just stare at the screen. I know I’ve done this a million times, but I suddenly have zero trust in what I just entered. I'll look at the screen and think, wait, did I ring this in for table 42 or table 24? Did I hit medium-rare or medium-well? And my mind just goes completely blank. It’s like the information is just slipping right out of my head the second I process it.

And it's not just the orders, either. Dave, my manager, he has me help out with the inventory sheets sometimes on Tuesday nights after we close. It's usually pretty straightforward—you go into the back room, count the liquor bottles, check the walk-in cooler, and write down the numbers on this big clipboard so he knows what to order from the distributors on Wednesday morning. But the last few weeks, I'll count a shelf of vodka, write down a twelve, and then just stare at the paper. I'll completely doubt myself. I'll have to recount the same shelf three or four times because I just can't hold the numbers in my head, and I don't trust my own eyes. 

It's so incredibly frustrating because, like I said, it should be muscle memory by now. But it takes me twice as long to do anything because I'm constantly deleting orders and starting over, or recounting boxes of takeout containers, just because my mind is so fogged up and slow. When the dinner rush hits and that kitchen printer is just spitting out tickets non-stop, you really can't afford to be standing there staring blankly at a computer screen, but I just can't seem to snap out of it and focus.
Would you say that you no longer take pleasure in activities you used to enjoy, even if you still participate in them?

Well, like I was saying a little bit ago, no, I wouldn't say that at all. It’s actually kind of the opposite when it comes to my hobbies and the things I do at home. I know I mentioned the vinyl records earlier, but it’s true for other things too. I’m not just going through the motions with my personal life the way I am when I'm carrying plates and taking orders at the restaurant. When I’m doing things I like, I genuinely still feel the joy from it. 

Like, take that Sunday breakfast I mentioned before. It's not just a chore, right? I don't just throw some frozen waffles in the toaster and stare at the wall. I actually really get into it. I’ll wake up early, even if I’m completely exhausted from a Saturday night closing shift where Dave kept us late rolling silverware and I didn't get out until past 1 AM. I'll go down to the kitchen, grind the coffee beans myself—we have this manual hand grinder that takes absolutely forever, but the coffee just tastes so much better, you know, it doesn't burn the beans like the electric ones do—and I’ll make a whole spread. 

I’ll do eggs over-medium, because my wife hates it when the yolk is too runny but she also hates when it's cooked completely solid, which is a really fine line to walk if you're not paying attention to the pan. And I'll get the bacon perfectly crispy. When we finally sit down at the little two-seater table by our kitchen window, and I take that first sip of coffee and see her enjoying the food... I feel actual happiness. Real pleasure. It’s not muted or grayed out or anything. It's like, for that half hour, that heavy, empty feeling in my chest that I was telling you about just lifts a little bit. 

So, no, if I'm doing something I love, the pleasure is definitely still there 100 percent. I haven't lost that spark for the good stuff, thank God. Because honestly, if I didn't have those little moments of actually enjoying my life and tasting my food and hearing the music, I really don't know how I'd get through the rest of the week with how foggy and weighed down I've been feeling everywhere else.
Have you noticed that your thoughts feel slowed down or that you’re having a hard time making decisions, even about small things like what to wear or what to eat?

Well, yeah, like I was telling you just a couple minutes ago with the computers at work—that's exactly it. That's exactly what I meant about my brain feeling like it's wading through mud. It’s that exact feeling of my thoughts just dragging and slowing down to an absolute crawl. 

When I'm standing there at the POS system, or doing those inventory sheets in the back cooler, I’m having so much trouble keeping the numbers straight. And like I said, I’ll literally just stare at the screen. I know I’ve done this for years, I know the menu inside and out, but I just don't trust what I just entered. And trying to make a decision on how to fix it, or even just deciding to hit the 'send' button to the kitchen printer? It's like a massive hurdle. I have to stand there and debate with myself over a simple table number because my brain just won't process it at a normal speed.

And you asked about the small stuff, like getting dressed... it's happening there, too. It really is. Like, getting dressed for my shift should be the easiest thing in the world. We have a strict uniform policy at the restaurant. Black pants, black non-slip shoes, and this specific maroon button-down shirt that Dave makes us wear. I have five of these maroon shirts hanging in my closet. They are completely identical. Literally the exact same brand, same size, same color, everything. But lately, I will stand there in front of the open closet door for five, maybe ten minutes, just staring at the hangers, trying to decide which identical shirt to put on. 

My wife will be calling up the stairs, asking if I'm ready to leave because she knows I hate being late, and my brain is just... buffering. I'll reach for the second shirt, then stop, then look at the fourth one, and I just can't make the call. Over a shirt! It’s ridiculous. But the gears up there are just turning so slowly right now. So yeah, whether it's trying to trust myself with the inventory numbers at work or just picking out clothes in the morning, every little thought and decision just feels like it takes ten times the effort it used to.
Have you noticed that your thoughts feel slowed down or that even small decisions take much longer to make than they used to?

I mean... yeah, like I literally just said a second ago, doc. I feel like I'm repeating myself a bit here, but yes, absolutely. It's exactly what I was just trying to explain about the POS system and those inventory sheets in the back. My brain is just dragging. I’m having so much trouble just keeping the numbers straight when I'm looking at them. 

I'll literally just stand there and stare at the screen, knowing full well I’ve done this exact same routine for years, but I just end up completely not trusting what I just entered. I'll punch in a normal order, and then I freeze. I have to stand there and debate with myself, like, did I hit the button for a side salad or fries? And even though my finger just left the touchscreen, the thought is just... gone. It's moving too slow to stick. It's honestly so frustrating to know you have all this experience doing something so simple, and suddenly you have to double and triple-check every single tap of your finger because your thoughts are moving at a snail's pace. So yeah, just deciding to hit 'send' on a ticket or writing down a number on the inventory clipboard takes way, way longer than it ever used to because I just can't trust my own head.
Have you experienced a loss of interest or pleasure in all activities, including those you used to enjoy?

Well, like I was telling you earlier—I feel like we're kind of going in circles here a bit, doc—but no, I haven't lost interest in everything. Not at all. Like I said about the Sunday breakfasts and my vinyl records, I still really enjoy the things I love doing. 

I mean, I don't want to repeat the whole story about the eggs and the bacon and the coffee grinder, but that's a perfect example. When I'm at home, and I'm putting on a record—lately I've been really into this original pressing of Fleetwood Mac's *Rumours* that I found at a flea market a couple weeks ago, the sleeve is a little beat up but the vinyl itself is pristine, barely a scratch on it—when I put that on, and I sit down with my wife, I genuinely feel good. I feel happy. I enjoy the music, I enjoy the food, I enjoy her company. 

It's just the work stuff, and the daily grind, and that heavy feeling I get when I'm not doing something I actively love. But the actual hobbies? The things that make me *me*? No, I still get a lot of pleasure out of those. If I didn't, like I said, I really don't know how I'd cope with the rest of it, with how slow and foggy my brain has been at the restaurant. So, no, definitely not a loss of pleasure in *everything*. Just... just in the things that feel like chores, I guess. But the good stuff is still good.
Have you experienced a loss of interest or pleasure in *all* activities, even those you used to enjoy most?

I... doc, I feel like I'm taking crazy pills here. Are you... are you reading off a list or something? Because I literally just answered this exact question like thirty seconds ago. 

I mean, I don't want to be difficult, I know you have a job to do, but I really feel like I'm just saying the same things over and over again. Like I just said, with the vinyl records and the Sunday breakfasts—no. No, I have not lost interest in all activities. I haven't. 

I was just explaining about the Fleetwood Mac record, the *Rumours* one I found at the flea market? The one with the pristine vinyl? When I put that on the turntable, and I hear that little crackle right before "Second Hand News" starts, and my wife is sitting there drinking her coffee... I still love that. I genuinely, truly enjoy it. It feels good. It feels like me. 

It's not everything that feels gray, you know? It's just the day-to-day stuff, the restaurant, the POS system, staring at those identical maroon shirts in my closet. That's the stuff that feels impossible and heavy. But my hobbies? The things I actually care about? I still look forward to them. I still get pleasure out of them. If I didn't have those moments, like sitting on the couch on a Sunday morning with the music playing, I don't know where I'd be. So, to answer your question again... no. I haven't lost interest in everything. Not at all.
Have you been having trouble sleeping, like waking up in the middle of the night or sleeping much more than usual?

No, actually, sleep is... sleep is one of the few things that's been totally fine. I mean, considering how... well, you know how exhausting the restaurant industry is, especially when we have a dinner rush and I'm on my feet for six, seven hours straight carrying those heavy oval trays. By the time I get home, my legs are just completely shot, so I'm pretty wiped out physically. 

Usually, I'll get in around 11:30 or midnight, depending on if I had to do the closing side-work—you know, rolling the silverware, marrying the ketchups, sweeping the server alley, all that tedious stuff that just drags on when you're already tired. And then I'll get home and take a quick shower just to get the smell of fryer grease and garlic off me, maybe watch like twenty minutes of whatever late-night show is on TV with my wife if she managed to stay awake for me, and then I'm out. I hit the pillow and I'm just out cold. 

We actually bought this really great mattress a few years ago, one of those thick memory foam ones, which honestly was an absolute game-changer for my lower back after being on my feet all day. So yeah, I sleep right through the night. I don't wake up at 3 AM staring at the ceiling or tossing and turning or anything like that. And I'm not oversleeping either. I usually wake up right around 8 or 8:30 naturally, even without an alarm, and I'll go make my coffee—like I mentioned with the grinder earlier—and start my day. So, no, honestly, my sleep schedule hasn't changed at all. It's been perfectly normal. It's just the waking hours where my brain feels like it's wading through molasses, if that makes sense. But the sleep itself? Totally fine.
Have you lost a noticeable amount of weight recently, even if you weren’t trying to go on a diet or change your eating habits?

Well, weight-wise, I haven't really stepped on a scale lately, but my eating has just been completely all over the place. It's really unpredictable right now. 

Like, at the restaurant, we get a staff meal before the dinner shift starts, usually around 4:30. The chefs will throw together something quick—like a big pan of baked ziti, or sometimes they'll use up the chicken breasts that are getting close to their date and make a huge salad. Normally, I'd eat a full plate because, you know, you need the energy to get through the night. But lately, there are weeks where I just look at it and I have zero appetite. I'll barely touch it. I'll just push a piece of lettuce around with my fork and drink a bunch of ice water, and my stomach just feels tight, like I couldn't swallow a bite if I tried. 

But then, the flip side of that is... I'll get through the whole shift running on empty, feeling that heavy, foggy feeling I told you about, and I'll get home at midnight. And suddenly, it's like a switch flips. I'll walk into my kitchen, and I just feel this need to eat everything in sight, just to feel... I don't know, settled? Grounded? Like, last Thursday, I came home and I ate half a box of stale Ritz crackers, two slices of leftover pizza cold right out of the fridge, and a bowl of cereal. It wasn't even that I was starving, exactly, it was just this weird compulsion to fill myself up so I could finally relax and go to sleep on that memory foam mattress I was telling you about. 

So, yeah, my appetite is just bouncing back and forth. One day I'm eating nothing for twelve hours, and the next I'm raiding the pantry at 1 AM like a teenager. I don't know if it's actually changed my weight, maybe my pants feel a little looser some days and tighter on others, but my eating habits are definitely not normal right now. It's just chaotic.
Have you experienced a loss of interest or pleasure in *all* activities, even those you used to enjoy most?

Doc, are you... are we doing some kind of loop here? Because I swear, I just answered this exact question like two minutes ago. Did you flip the page back by accident or something? 

I mean, I don't want to be disrespectful, I know you've got your clipboard and your checklist and all that, but I feel like I'm repeating myself. Like I said before—with the Fleetwood Mac record, the vinyl I found at the flea market? The one I put on the turntable on Sunday mornings while my wife drinks her coffee? I still love that.
